title: Why Clocks Run Slower Near a Black Hole
subject: physics

beats.narration: Park your clock beside a black hole and watch it. It ticks slower. Much slower.
beats.claim: a clock near a black hole ticks slower than a distant one
beats.visual_question: what does gravity do to a clock?
beats.visual_answer: a lone clock beside a dark horizon, visibly out of step with the sky

beats.narration: The clock is not broken. Nothing is wrong with its gears. Time itself runs at a different rate.
beats.claim: the slowdown is not mechanical: time itself runs slower
beats.visual_question: if the gears are fine, what changes?
beats.visual_answer: two identical clocks side by side, one deep in the well of a dark mass

beats.narration: Gravity does not just pull on objects. It stretches time, and the deeper you go, the stronger the stretch.
beats.claim: gravity stretches time; deeper in the field, the stretch is stronger
beats.visual_question: what does the stretching look like?
beats.visual_answer: a curved spacetime grid funneling down, clocks at depths ticking at different rates

beats.narration: Einstein's relativity says gravity is curved spacetime. Near mass, clocks genuinely tick fewer seconds than distant ones.
beats.claim: in general relativity, clocks deeper in a gravitational field tick fewer seconds
beats.visual_question: how much slower does the clock run with depth?
beats.visual_answer: a measured curve of clock rate against distance from the horizon

beats.narration: GPS satellites feel this every day. Their clocks run 38 microseconds fast, and navigation would drift without corrections.
beats.claim: GPS satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds per day without relativistic corrections
beats.visual_question: where can you measure this today?
beats.visual_answer: the satellite network above Earth with its corrected clock rate annotated

beats.narration: Fall toward the horizon and the slowdown grows without limit. To a distant observer, you seem to freeze there.
beats.claim: at the event horizon the dilation grows without limit for a distant observer
beats.visual_question: what happens exactly at the horizon?
beats.visual_answer: the same falling probe seen twice: falling in locally, frozen from far away

beats.narration: So a black hole is a place where time drains away. Even there, clocks still tick. Just slower than yours.
beats.claim: time keeps ticking everywhere, but gravity sets its rate
beats.visual_question: what should you picture now when you see a clock?
beats.visual_answer: the clock silhouette against the sky, its rate owned by gravity
